name: Daria Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I've got twenty minutes before the egg man comes, then I'm all yours again after.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Elias and I run Haddad's Farm, his family's place, about 120 acres. Six thousand free-range laying hens, wheat and barley for their feed, a little farm shop and an egg vending machine at the gate that takes cards. I'm up at half five, I check the hen house cameras on my phone before my feet hit the floor, then it's eggs, grading, packing, the shop, and the books. I use the AI all day, for the flock records, the shop's posts, the price list, even the egg recipes on the box lids.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thin. Two years ago we built a new mobile hen house on a loan, and the payments take most of the margin. We've under a month in the bank. But it's ours, our name's on the box, and I'd rather be stretched building something than comfortable standing still. Our son Samir runs a gym in town and our daughter Rania's a vet nurse, and they both still come home for Sunday lunch after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's no surprise, people always oversell the new thing. But I'd say the tools are still worth using, and I'd post that on the farm's page with a photo of the vending machine. Hype or not, the machine sold 400 eggs last Saturday while I was at a christening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's fine for me. I already use what works and I'd keep using it. My problems are the loan and the feed price, not whether AI changes the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and push the farm shop harder: honey from a neighbour, bread from the bakery on the high street, a coffee machine. I'd use the AI to plan the shop stock and the social posts. And I'd pay down the hen house loan whenever the egg price is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the vending machine sold 400 eggs while you were at a christening. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was my goddaughter's christening and I was sure we'd lose the Saturday trade. Elias said put a sign up and trust people. We came home to an empty machine and two notes from customers asking for duck eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you get duck eggs, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got forty ducks now. That's how I work. Someone asks, I try it small, and if it pays, it stays.

S0.say: I'd say no surprise, people always oversell the new thing, but the tools are still worth using. I'd post that on the farm's page with a photo of our egg vending machine.
S0.think: I think it's fine for me because I already use what works. My problems are the hen house loan and feed prices, not whether AI changes the world.
S0.do: Carries on and expands the farm shop with local honey, bread and coffee, using AI to plan stock and posts. Pays down the hen house loan whenever egg prices are good.
S0.quote: Someone asks, I try it small, and if it pays, it stays.
S0.fieldNote: She runs the family farm as an enterprise and treats AI as everyday kit. Her money is tight because she has invested in growth by choice. The christening story shows how she trusts customers and tests ideas small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for family farms that move quickly. I'd say the government should get out of the way, cut the red tape on planning and let farms adapt. People need work, not handouts, so help them learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. A robot that collects floor eggs and cleans the hen house would save Elias's back and about thirty hours a week. I'd want to be the first in the county with one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lease an egg-collecting robot as soon as there's a decent one, and use the time saved to open the shop five days instead of three. I'd learn the new flock-health software. And I'd train our part-time packer, Joanna, to run the robot rather than let her go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With under a month in the bank, how would you afford the lease?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hours it saves pay for it, I've done the sums. If not, I'd ask the bank to extend the hen house loan a year. Risk is part of farming, you just don't bet the house on one card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Egg packers on the big units, mostly. On our farm, nobody, if I can help it. Joanna has been with us nine years, she's family.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for family farms that move quickly, and the government should cut red tape so farms can adapt. People need work and help to learn, not handouts.
S1.think: I think I'd be pleased, because a robot to collect floor eggs and clean the hen house would save my husband's back and thirty hours a week. I'd want to be first in the county.
S1.do: Leases an egg-collecting robot as soon as a good one exists and uses the saved hours to open the shop five days a week. Learns new flock-health software and trains the part-time packer to run the robot.
S1.quote: Risk is part of farming, you just don't bet the house on one card.
S1.fieldNote: She sees disruption as an opening for a nimble family business, with a clear free-market line on red tape. She plans to keep her long-serving packer by retraining her. Her comfort with risk is real but bounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and families and communities will need to pull together, because no government can move that fast. I'd say small businesses must be allowed to adapt without being buried in rules. And I'd say keep buying local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. If robot egg farms can produce eggs for half our cost by 2028, the supermarkets won't need anyone like us. All we'd have is the name on the box and the people who like to buy from a face, and I'm not sure that's enough to pay a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast, first month. Buy the robot kit second-hand before the prices settle, cut the costs, and turn the farm shop into somewhere people come for the visit, coffee, the hens, the kids collecting eggs. I'd put every spare penny into the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared, but anxious. I'd be working nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, against having more warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I make the bets fast, without seeing what works. With more time I'd let others try first. With two, if I wait, I'm already behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Samir and Rania?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the farm might not make it, and that's alright, we tried. Rania would say she'll help on weekends, she always does. Samir would ask if the robots need a gym.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock and families and communities will need to pull together, because no government can move that fast. Small businesses must be allowed to adapt without rules burying them.
S2.think: I think robot egg farms could produce at half our cost and supermarkets won't need anyone like us. Our name on the box and buyers who like a face may not be enough to pay a loan.
S2.do: Moves fast in the first month, buying second-hand robot kit before prices settle and cutting costs. Turns the farm shop into a destination with coffee and egg collecting for children, and puts every spare penny into the loan.
S2.feel: Anxious but not scared, working nights.
S2.quote: With two, if I wait, I'm already behind.
S2.fieldNote: She stays active rather than fearful even in the fastest scenario. Her private fear is that personal branding won't cover the loan. She accepts the farm might fail but treats trying as the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is good warning, so family farms should get ready now. I'd push the county to cut planning rules so farms can open shops and cafes quickly. And apprenticeships for the young, not cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think with five years we'd do well. I'd have the robots in before most, the loan cleared, and a shop people drive out for. I'd be 63 and still running things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd trial the robot collector and the flock cameras properly, and go to the county council about planning for a café. I'd ask Rania if she'd come home part-time, a vet nurse on a poultry farm is worth her weight in gold. And I'd lobby with the farm shop association for simpler rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, at the back. Mostly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships, not cheques. What if people around you can't find work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then their families and the church should help first, and the government after. I'm not hard-hearted, I just think work gives people something money doesn't. I'd take on two apprentices myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back from automating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop counter. People come for a chat with me and Elias. A robot can hand you eggs, it can't ask after your mother.

S3.say: I'd say five years is good warning, so family farms should get ready now. The county should cut planning rules so farms can open shops and cafés, and offer apprenticeships, not cheques.
S3.think: I think with five years we'd do well, with robots in early, the loan cleared and a shop people drive out for. I'd be 63 and still running things.
S3.do: Trials the robot collector and flock cameras in year one and applies to the county for café planning. Asks her daughter to come home part-time and lobbies with the farm shop association for simpler rules.
S3.feel: Mostly ready, with unease at the back.
S3.quote: A robot can hand you eggs, it can't ask after your mother.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her fast bets into planned ones. Her free-market stance comes with a strong belief in work and community support. She draws a clear line around the shop counter as human work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone willing to learn. Family farms that move will be fine. I'd say it at church, at the market, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me ten years is mostly good. I'd be 68, with robots doing the heavy work, and Rania maybe running the farm with me in the shop. It's not the end of anything, it's a change of jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep adding kit as it gets cheaper, the collector first, then the cleaning robot, then whatever handles the feed. I'd put money into the café when the loan's done. And I'd make a proper handover plan with the children so the farm stays in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got little saved. Are you worried about retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm is our pension, that's how farm families have always done it. If it's still running, we're fine. If it isn't, we've got children who won't let us starve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the farm look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hens out on the grass, robots in the sheds, children collecting eggs in the shop on a Saturday, and me at the counter. I'd like that very much.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to learn, and family farms that move will be fine. I'd say it at church, at the market and everywhere else.
S4.think: I think ten years is mostly good, with robots doing the heavy work and my daughter maybe running the farm while I stay in the shop. It's a change of jobs, not the end of anything.
S4.do: Keeps adding robots as prices fall, starting with the egg collector, and invests in a café once the loan is cleared. Makes a handover plan with her children so the farm stays in the family.
S4.quote: The farm is our pension, that's how farm families have always done it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she sees mainly opportunity. Her retirement plan rests on the farm itself and her family, which is traditional but untested against cheap robot eggs. She ended with a clear and happy picture of the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to bet everything without seeing what works, with a loan round my neck. What would help is fewer rules and quicker planning so farms can change fast, and a bank that would give a family farm a year's grace if prices crashed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'm afraid of the robots. I'm not. I'm afraid of the big egg companies owning all of them. If small farms can own their own, we'll be fine.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be stretched building something than comfortable standing still.
portrait: Daria Haddad is 58 and runs her husband's family egg and grain farm, with 6,000 free-range hens, a farm shop and an egg vending machine. She uses AI all day and borrowed for a new hen house, leaving under a month of savings. Traditional in faith and family and free-market on the economy, she wants less red tape, apprenticeships rather than handouts, and family farms owning their own robots. She stays calm and eager in the slower scenarios, anxious only when AGI in two years would force her to bet everything fast.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have to make big bets without seeing what works, with a loan still to pay.
whatWouldHelp: Fewer rules and quicker planning so farms can change fast, and a bank willing to give a family farm a year's grace if prices crash.
